issue: Can a nonretroactive change in sentencing law, whether by statute or guidelines amendment, be an extraordinary and compelling reason for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A)?

sides.position: A nonretroactive change in law cannot be an extraordinary and compelling reason, because nonretroactivity is ordinary and serving a lawfully imposed sentence is routine
cases: United States v. McCall, 56 F.4th 1048 (6th Cir. 2022) (en banc)
United States v. Andrews, 12 F.4th 255 (3d Cir. 2021)
United States v. Thacker, 4 F.4th 569 (7th Cir. 2021)
United States v. Maumau, 993 F.3d 821 (10th Cir. 2021) (Tymkovich, C.J., concurring)
United States v. Crandall, 25 F.4th 582 (8th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Rodrigo Rodriguez-Mendez, 65 F.4th 1000 (8th Cir. 2023)

sides.position: A nonretroactive change in law can be considered as an extraordinary and compelling reason for relief

this_court: does not decide (notes that Crandall previously sided with the McCall side of the split)
quote: There is also a circuit split on the merits of whether a nonretroactive change in the law -- whether by statute or by guidelines amendment -- can constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason for § 3582(c)(1)(A) relief.
cite: United States v. Rodrigo Rodriguez-Mendez, 65 F.4th 1000 (8th Cir. 2023)
